title: Metals and Reactivity
description: The reactivity series, displacement and how metals are extracted.
hero_image_caption: From ancient iron smelting to modern phytomining, the chemistry of metal extraction has shaped civilisation.
content_html:
The Reactivity Series

Different metals react with different levels of vigour with water, oxygen and acids. Chemists arrange metals in order of this reactivity to produce the reactivity series. From most to least reactive, the key metals to know are:

Potassium (K) → Sodium (Na) → Calcium (Ca) → Magnesium (Mg) → Aluminium (Al) → Carbon (C) → Zinc (Zn) → Iron (Fe) → Hydrogen (H) → Copper (Cu) → Silver (Ag) → Gold (Au)

Carbon and hydrogen are not metals, but they are included as reference points because they are important in extraction reactions. Metals above hydrogen in the series react with dilute acids to produce hydrogen gas; metals below hydrogen do not. The most reactive metals (potassium, sodium) react explosively with cold water, while moderately reactive metals like magnesium react slowly with cold water but vigorously with steam.

Key Fact

Reactivity series (most to least): K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, C, Zn, Fe, H, Cu, Ag, Au. Metals above carbon need electrolysis to extract; metals below carbon can be extracted by reduction with carbon. Metals above hydrogen react with acids to give H₂ gas.

Displacement Reactions

A more reactive metal will displace a less reactive metal from a solution of one of its compounds. This is a practical way to confirm relative reactivity. For example, placing iron into copper sulfate solution displaces copper, because iron is higher in the reactivity series:

$$Fe(s) + CuSO_4(aq) \rightarrow FeSO_4(aq) + Cu(s)$$

Observations: the iron becomes coated with a reddish-brown layer of copper, and the blue colour of the solution fades as copper(II) ions are removed and replaced with paler iron(II) ions. Displacement reactions are also redox reactions — the more reactive metal is oxidised (loses electrons) and the metal ion in solution is reduced (gains electrons).

In the iron/copper displacement reaction, iron atoms each lose two electrons: \(Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-\) — this is oxidation. The copper ions each gain two electrons: \(Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu\) — this is reduction. Remember: OIL RIG — Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain.

You can write ionic half-equations for each electrode process separately, then combine them to give the overall ionic equation.

Extracting Metals from Their Ores

Metals are found in the Earth's crust, often combined with other elements in ores. The method of extraction depends on the metal's position in the reactivity series. Metals that are less reactive than carbon can be extracted by heating their oxide with carbon — the carbon removes the oxygen (reduction):

$$2Fe_2O_3(s) + 3C(s) \rightarrow 4Fe(l) + 3CO_2(g)$$

This reaction occurs in a blast furnace. Iron ore (haematite, \(Fe_2O_3\)), coke (carbon) and limestone (\(CaCO_3\)) are added at the top. Hot air is blasted in at the bottom. The coke burns to form carbon monoxide, which reduces the iron oxide to molten iron that trickles to the bottom and is tapped off. Limestone removes acidic impurities (silica) as molten slag.

Key Fact

Metals below carbon in the reactivity series (e.g. iron, copper, zinc) are extracted by reduction with carbon — cheaper but limited. Metals above carbon (e.g. aluminium, sodium) must be extracted by electrolysis — more expensive because it uses large amounts of electricity.

Biological Methods of Metal Extraction

Traditional mining is expensive and environmentally damaging. Low-grade ores — where metal concentrations are too low to justify conventional extraction — can instead be processed using biological methods. Two important techniques are phytomining and bioleaching.

In phytomining, specific plant species (called hyperaccumulators) are grown on soil containing low-grade metal ore. The plants draw metal ions up through their roots and store them in leaves and stems. When the crop is harvested and incinerated, the ash contains a concentrated form of the metal compound, which is then processed to obtain the metal. The technique is slow but has a much lower environmental footprint than open-cast mining.

In bioleaching, certain bacteria (such as Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans) are used to break down metal sulfide ores. The bacteria oxidise the sulfide minerals, releasing metal ions into an acidic solution called a leachate. The metal is then recovered from the leachate by displacement — scrap iron is added to displace copper, for example, because iron is higher in the reactivity series: \(Fe(s) + CuSO_4(aq) \rightarrow FeSO_4(aq) + Cu(s)\).

Bioleaching produces acidic waste water that can pollute nearby rivers and streams — a significant environmental concern that requires careful management. However, compared with conventional smelting, it avoids the production of sulfur dioxide air pollution.

Key Fact

Phytomining: grow hyperaccumulator plants on low-grade ore → harvest and burn → recover metal from ash. Bioleaching: bacteria break down ore → metal ions in leachate → recover metal by displacement with scrap iron. Both are lower-impact alternatives to traditional mining.

Recycling Metals

Recycling metals saves energy — often a large fraction of the energy required compared with extracting from ore — and conserves finite ore reserves. It also reduces waste going to landfill and cuts the environmental damage from mining operations. However, sorting and collection of scrap metal has its own costs, and contamination can reduce the quality of recycled metal. Despite this, recycling aluminium, for example, uses a small fraction of the energy that electrolysis of aluminium ore demands.
exam_tip_html: Displacement and extraction questions almost always begin with 'use the reactivity series to explain'. Make sure you can recall the full series, place carbon and hydrogen correctly, and explain that a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive one. For biological extraction, remember the two named methods — phytomining and bioleaching — and be ready to compare their environmental advantages and disadvantages against conventional mining.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The reactivity series orders metals from most to least reactive. A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compound in a displacement (redox) reaction.
  • Metals below carbon in the series are extracted by reduction with carbon (e.g. iron in a blast furnace); metals above carbon require electrolysis.
  • Phytomining (plants absorb metal ions) and bioleaching (bacteria break down ore) allow recovery of metals from low-grade ores with lower environmental impact than conventional mining.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following metals can be extracted from its ore by reduction with carbon?
A) Potassium
B) Sodium
C) Aluminium
D) Copper
practice_questions.marks: D) Copper [1 mark] — copper is below carbon in the reactivity series.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a 'displacement reaction' and give one example using named metals.
practice_questions.marks: A reaction where a more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal in a compound [1]; e.g. zinc + copper sulfate → zinc sulfate + copper (or other valid example with correct reactivity direction) [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe how iron is extracted from iron ore in a blast furnace. Include the names of the raw materials added and the process by which iron is produced.
practice_questions.marks: Iron ore (haematite/Fe₂O₃), coke (carbon) and limestone are added [1]; hot air is blasted in and carbon burns to form carbon monoxide [1]; carbon (or carbon monoxide) reduces iron oxide to molten iron, which is tapped from the bottom of the furnace [1].

practice_questions.text: A mining company wants to recover copper from a large area of land where the ore concentration is too low for conventional mining. Explain how phytomining could be used to extract the copper, including what happens to the copper after the plants are harvested.
practice_questions.marks: Hyperaccumulator plants are grown on the low-grade ore / soil [1]; the plants absorb copper ions through their roots and accumulate them in leaves/stems [1]; the plants are harvested and burned / incinerated [1]; copper compounds are concentrated in the ash and processed to obtain the metal [1].

practice_questions.text: A student compares extracting copper by smelting (heating ore with carbon) with bioleaching. Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of bioleaching from both an economic and an environmental perspective.
practice_questions.marks: StudyVault Mastering: Environmental advantages of bioleaching — avoids SO₂ air pollution from smelting [1]; can use low-grade ore that would otherwise be uneconomical [1]; Environmental disadvantages — produces acidic leachate that can pollute water sources [1]; requires management to prevent contamination [1]; Economic: lower energy costs and avoids expensive smelting equipment [1]; however, process is slow and requires bacterial maintenance [1]. Secure: four points with some weighing of evidence. Developing: two relevant points without comparative evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Explain, using the reactivity series, why magnesium displaces copper from copper sulfate solution but copper does not displace magnesium from magnesium sulfate solution. Include the ionic equation for the displacement reaction between magnesium and copper sulfate.
practice_questions.marks: StudyVault Mastering: magnesium is higher in the reactivity series than copper [1]; more reactive metals displace less reactive metals from their compounds [1]; copper cannot displace magnesium because copper is less reactive [1]; ionic equation: Mg + Cu²⁺ → Mg²⁺ + Cu [1]; Mg is oxidised (loses electrons) and Cu²⁺ is reduced (gains electrons) [1]. Secure: first four points. Developing: states Mg more reactive and writes word equation only.

knowledge_checks.q: Which metal is the MOST reactive in the reactivity series?
Why must aluminium be extracted by electrolysis rather than by reduction with carbon?
options: Aluminium does not form an oxide
Aluminium is above carbon in the reactivity series
Aluminium does not react with electricity
Carbon is more expensive than electricity

knowledge_checks.q: In phytomining, what do the plants do with metal ions from the soil: _____
options: Absorb and accumulate them in their tissues
Break them down into pure metal
knowledge_checks.explanation: The correct answer is Absorb and accumulate them in their tissues.

knowledge_checks.q: When iron is added to copper sulfate solution, which observation confirms that a displacement reaction has occurred: _____
options: A reddish-brown coating forms on the iron
The iron dissolves completely with no colour change
knowledge_checks.explanation: The correct answer is A reddish-brown coating forms on the iron.

knowledge_checks.explanation: Review the key terms and definitions covered in this lesson.

flashcard_questions.a: A list of metals arranged in order of reactivity from most reactive (potassium) to least reactive (gold), used to predict displacement reactions and extraction methods.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens in a displacement reaction?
flashcard_questions.a: A more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal in a compound, releasing the less reactive metal as an element.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are metals above carbon in the reactivity series extracted by electrolysis?
flashcard_questions.a: Because carbon is not reactive enough to displace them from their compounds — electrolysis is needed to force the reaction using electrical energy.
A method of metal extraction where hyperaccumulator plants are grown on low-grade ore, absorbing metal ions into their tissues.
A method where bacteria break down low-grade metal ore, releasing metal ions into an acidic leachate. The metal is then recovered by displacement with a more reactive metal.

flashcard_questions.q: What raw materials are added to a blast furnace?
flashcard_questions.a: Iron ore (haematite), coke (carbon) and limestone. Hot air is blasted in to drive the reduction of iron oxide to molten iron.

flashcard_questions.q: In a displacement reaction, which metal is oxidised?
flashcard_questions.a: The more reactive metal — it loses electrons to the less reactive metal ion in solution.

glossary_terms.definition: A list of metals arranged in order of reactivity, from most reactive (potassium) to least reactive (gold). Position determines how a metal is extracted and how it behaves in displacement reactions.
A reaction where a more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal in a compound, releasing the less reactive metal as an element.
A rock containing enough metal compound to make extraction economically worthwhile.
The gain of electrons, or the removal of oxygen from a compound. In metal extraction, metal oxides are reduced to metals by carbon.
A large industrial furnace used to extract iron from iron ore by reduction with carbon. Iron ore, coke and limestone are added, and hot air is blasted in to drive the reactions.
A method of extracting metals from low-grade ores using plants that absorb and accumulate metal ions. The plants are harvested and burned, and the metal is recovered from the ash.
A method of extracting metals from low-grade ores using bacteria that break down metal sulfide minerals, releasing metal ions into a leachate solution from which the metal is then recovered.
The loss of electrons (or gain of oxygen) by a substance in a chemical reaction.
A reaction in which oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously — one substance loses electrons and another gains them.
